title: The rich fool (Luke 12:16–21)
hook: a man plans bigger barns for his surplus and dies that night

segments.voice: A talent was a weight of silver, and the servant who buried his did it out of fear.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. Jesus won't referee. He tells a story instead. A rich man's land has a bumper year, more grain than his barns can hold. He lies awake, talking it over with himself. What shall I do? I know: I'll tear down my barns and build bigger ones. I'll store everything. Then I'll say to my soul: you're set for years. Eat, drink, enjoy. It's a good plan. Any financial advisor would sign off on it. And that same night, God speaks to him, for the only time in the story, and calls him a fool.
screen: `SPLIT THE INHERITANCE.` → `A BUMPER YEAR.` → `BIGGER BARNS.` → `THAT SAME NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Hear him: my crops, my barns, my fruits, my goods, my soul. I, my and mine, again and again. Nobody else is in the plan: no family, no workers, no neighbor. He even talks to his own soul, as if it's the only one in the room. The old King James Bible gives his words: "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry." And the answer: "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?" He isn't a thief or a cheat; the land just produced. Saving isn't the problem either: the Bible praises the ant for storing food. His mistake is quieter. He thinks the barn is his life. Jesus says it plainly just before the story: a man's life doesn't consist in the abundance of the things he owns. And fool here doesn't mean stupid; he's clearly clever. In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there. Whose? He's about to leave it all to someone else, which is exactly what the brother in the crowd was fighting over. Luke ends with one more line: so is anyone who stores up treasure for himself and isn't rich toward God. Christians have heard rich toward God as generosity, prayer, a life turned outward. Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give.
screen: `I, MY, MINE.` · `NOT A THIEF. NOT A CHEAT.` · `HE THINKS THE BARN IS HIS LIFE.` · `WHOSE SHALL THOSE THINGS BE?` · then, large: `RICH TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: Walk through your home in your mind: the closet, the drawer you never open. Find one thing you keep just to keep it, like a coat you never wear, and picture who could use it. If you pray, ask where it should go; if not, just picture it leaving your barn and landing where it's needed.
Fool. Not stupid, in the Bible's sense, but someone who lives as if God weren't there, like the man building bigger barns for a life only he controlled.
Your line: you can't take the barn. But you can be rich toward God. Thirty days now, a whole month.

howItsDone: Many Christians read this parable as a warning against greed and a call to generosity, and it's often preached alongside giving to the poor, tithing, or simplifying how they live.

what a scholar hears: aphrōn, fool, the word the Psalms use for someone who lives as if there is no God. and the question it ends on, whose shall those things be, answers the brother fighting over an inheritance.
recall: a picture thrown beside the real thing
euangelion: good news, announced to all

chat.says: Why does God call the man with the bigger barns a fool? Saving's smart, right?
options: Saving's fine. He lived as if God weren't there, and thought the barn was his life.
He was a cheat who got his big harvest by stealing from his workers.
Because the Bible says saving anything for later is always wrong.
chat.meaning: In the Bible a fool lives as if God weren't there. Saving isn't the problem; he thought the barn was his life.

notes: 'The Bible praises the ant for storing food' refers to Proverbs 6:6–8; confirm the aside is welcome.

'In the Bible a fool is someone who lives as if God weren't there' leans on Psalm 14:1 / 53:1 ('The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God'). The Greek Septuagint of Psalm 14:1 uses ἄφρων; please confirm the trapdoor link.
'Luke's answer, a few verses on, is simple: give' refers to Luke 12:33 (sell what you have and give alms); paraphrased. Confirm.
Count of 'I / my' is left unnumbered ('again and again') on purpose; the KJV has many first-person pronouns in 12:17–19.
Hook: 'God speaks to him, for the only time in the story' — God speaks only once in the parable; confirm wording.
